objections.gloss: Marquis locates the wrong of killing in the deprivation of a future-like-ours, which the fetus has regardless of personhood — so abortion inflicts the very wrong that makes killing wrong. Grant it…
objections.title: The objection refuses both horns this wing splits. It does not claim the fetus is a person, and it does not let non-personhood trivialize the loss. With Marquis, it locates the wrong of killing in the deprivation of a future-like-ours — a future of valuable experiences, projects, and enjoyments — and observes that the fetus has exactly such a future, owed to the deprivation itself rather than to any present status. So abortion inflicts the very wrong that makes killing wrong, and a duty not to inflict it is meant to ground a constraint the bodily-sovereignty default has not yet answered: a constraint resting on the value of the future, the one lever none of the four standing nodes engages.

objections.gloss: The use of one's own body as life-support for another is, by default, the body-holder's to grant or withhold — so the burden falls on whoever would compel its continued use, not on the pregnant…
objections.title: The objection challenges the burden's direction. A pregnancy, it says, is not a purely private matter on the order of a haircut or a career change: it involves a developing human life, a second party whose stake is the gravest possible. Given that, the default cannot run in favor of termination-on-request. The presumption must favor continuation — the pregnant person who would end the pregnancy bears the burden of justification, not the party who would see it preserved. To treat "her body, her call" as the starting point is to beg the question against the second party by assuming away its standing before the argument has begun. The right placement of the burden is on the chooser to show why the pregnancy may be ended, not on the objector to show why it may not.

objections.gloss: Responsibility for another's need grounds a duty of aid, not a duty to supply one's body — and gestation is the supply of a body. Grant in full that the pregnant person voluntarily created the…
objections.title: The objection turns on a disanalogy the bodily-sovereignty default is said to ignore. Thomson's hostage was kidnapped — wired to the violinist without lifting a finger — whereas the pregnant person, in the ordinary case, voluntarily performed the very act that brings the dependent into being, knowing pregnancy to be its foreseeable result. One who knowingly undertakes an action that creates a dependent, the objection runs, assumes responsibility for that dependent, and assumed responsibilities ground duties. The fetus, moreover, exists only because of her act and depends on her body alone; she has created not merely a need but an exclusive need, and to walk away is not the mere declining of aid a stranger may decline but the abandonment of a dependent one has made. So the bodily-sovereignty default is defeated for the ordinary case: voluntary responsibility converts what would otherwise be a permissible withdrawal into a forbidden one, and the analogy to refusing a kidney one never undertook to provide simply does not reach her.

objections.gloss: The objection has two parts: terminating wrongs the one who would have lived, depriving it of a future of goods, so 'abortion wrongs no one' is false; and the suite, by appraising the act at all…
objections.title: The objection grants what the optionality layer has won and resists on new ground: even if the competent pregnant person holds an unassailable right to choose, the suite must stay silent on the act's worth, as it does in every other wing, and to say abortion is good is both false and illicit. False, because terminating deprives the being who would have lived of a future of goods, so there is a victim and the act wrongs someone. Illicit, because the suite's entire meta-defense rests on its appraisal-silence over contested acts; to appraise here, even advisorily, is to break by one's own hand the firewall one's capstone certified. So the positive claim, the objection concludes, either asserts a falsehood about a victim or forfeits the architecture that lets the suite defend rights without endorsing acts.

objections.gloss: The objection's handle is the positive reason — that abortion spares a would-be person existence's guaranteed harms — and its charge is that, since harm admits of degree, the reason grades lives by…
objections.title: The moment the suite asserts a positive moral appraisal of abortion — not merely the right to it, but that abortion wrongs no one and that antinatalism supplies a reason in its favor — it steps onto the slope toward judging which lives are worth living. The positive reason offered is harm-prevention: abortion spares a would-be person the guaranteed harms of existence. But harm is not uniform. A pregnancy carrying a severe, foreseeable burden of suffering would, on the suite's own logic, give a stronger reason for termination than an ordinary one — and now the suite grades lives by their projected harm-load, leaning hardest against the lives that would suffer most. That is the structure of eugenics: the ranking of existences by worth, the marking of some lives as better never lived. The non-comparative label the suite attaches does not save it — one may grant that the consideration applies to every conception and still note that it applies with graded force, and the gradient is the selection. The appraisal cannot stay universal once its own reason admits of degree.

objections.gloss: Grant the killing/letting-die distinction its full weight — unplug the violinist and he dies of his own renal failure, permitted; stab him and you add a killing, not. It grips that case only because…
objections.title: The objection concedes the ground already taken — that bodies are not conscriptable, that voluntary sex grounds no duty to gestate — and resists at the one point those concessions leave open: the manner of the act. Bodily sovereignty, on Thomson's own analysis, licenses withdrawing the use of one's body. You unplug yourself from the violinist and he dies, but of his own kidney ailment, not your hand; you have declined to go on serving as his life-support, which is your right, and his pre-existing condition does the rest. Abortion, the objection presses, is frequently nothing so passive. To dismember a fetus, or to induce its demise before removal, is not to cease lending a body but to actively end a life — and the right not to sustain another is not a right to kill him. The killing/letting-die distinction is a weighty moral primitive: you may unplug the violinist, you may not reach over and stab him, though he dies either way. So even granting the bodily-sovereignty default in full, the objection concludes, the manner of abortion forfeits the right wherever it crosses from withdrawing support into actively killing the dependent — a line the violinist analogy draws and most abortions cross.

objections.gloss: The right does not turn on whether the fetus is a person, because it holds either way — and a claim that holds on both answers to a question does not depend on the question. If the fetus is not a…
objections.title: The objection insists the entire question turns on a single metaphysical fact: the moral status of the fetus. Whether abortion may be chosen, it says, depends wholly on whether the fetus is a person. If it is a person, then ending the pregnancy ends a person's life, and no consideration drawn from the pregnant person's body can convert a homicide into a permissible act — the right collapses into a license to kill. If it is not a person, the right is genuine but empty, a permission opposed by no one and needing no defense. Either way, the objection presses, the personhood question is dispositive, and a defense that will not answer it has skipped the one step on which everything depends. A suite that routes around fetal status, in this telling, has not defended the right; it has changed the subject.
